paragraphs: Software firms that once sold programs outright now mostly rent them by the month, and the change is usually explained as a convenience to customers. Its effect on the firms' revenue is subtler. A purchase yields a large payment up front and little afterward, so a firm's income swings with each release cycle. A subscription spreads the same money across years, which steadies income and makes it easier to forecast, but it also means that a dissatisfied customer can leave at any time, rather than only after the next upgrade. Firms that have switched report higher lifetime revenue per customer on average, but this may reflect the kinds of customers who remain, since those who found the new terms unattractive have gone. Whether subscription pricing makes a product better, rather than merely more profitable, is a separate matter that revenue figures cannot settle.
